item.title: Explainer: How will midterm election results affect U.S. foreign policy?
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05
WASHINGTON, Nov. 5 (Xinhua) -- The Democrats' sweeping victory in the U.S. midterm elections could give the party greater leverage to challenge President Donald Trump's policies, but the extent of their influence remains uncertain. With Democrats poised to take control of Congress, the party is expected to step up scrutiny of Trump's military actions against Iran, seek to roll back some of his tariffs and push for stronger support for Ukraine. However, the president's executive authority and veto power, along with persistent political divisions inside the Beltway, could limit the extent to which Democrats can translate their electoral gains into concrete policy changes. ON IRAN WAR The Republican losses in the midterm elections have intensified scrutiny of Trump's decision to launch the war against Iran, raising questions about whether the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress could exert greater pressure on the administration to bring the conflict to an end. People close to Trump have blamed the war for contributing to the Republican defeat, with some White House officials and Republican allies reportedly arguing that the conflict was misguided, The Wall Street Journal reported. Trump himself acknowledged that the war was partly responsible for the party's losses, although he said he did not regret launching it. The election outcome could give Democrats greater leverage to challenge the administration's approach to the conflict. That leverage could take several forms. Democrats could push for further votes on war powers resolutions, which seek to limit or terminate unauthorized military operations, or use the appropriations process to restrict funding for prolonging the conflict. Colorado Democratic Rep. Jason Crow, a member of the House Armed Services Committee, told CBS News that lawmakers had already voted on seven resolutions concerning the conflict, with two passing so far, arguing that Congress should continue holding votes. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, on the other hand, said Wednesday that the incoming majority could use Congress' control over federal spending to pressure Trump to end the war. "The American people don't know what the heck we're fighting for in Iran," Schumer told journalists, later noting that the "power of the purse" is "one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people." However, congressional opposition does not automatically translate into an end to military operations. The president retains substantial authority over military command and foreign policy, while legislative efforts to restrict military action could face procedural and political obstacles. Under the War Powers Resolution, a federal law passed in 1973, the president, after notifying Congress of the use of military force, must terminate the action within 60 days unless Congress authorizes continued military action. The president can then issue a veto, which can only be overcome by a two-thirds supermajority in both the House and Senate. Despite the sweeping victory in the midterm elections, Democrats are well short of those supermajority thresholds. Whether Democrats can turn their electoral gains into an effective constraint on Trump's Iran policy will therefore depend on their ability to secure sufficient support for funding restrictions or war powers legislation. ON TARIFFS The Democrats' gains in the midterm elections could give the party new opportunities to challenge Trump's tariff policies, but their ability to reverse the measures is likely to be constrained by the president's veto power and the administration's reliance on executive authority. Democrats are expected to push for legislation to repeal some of Trump's tariffs and reform the laws that have allowed him to impose duties with limited congressional involvement. One of the most obvious priorities would be repealing Trump's tariffs on Canada, which are raising prices and harming communities on both sides of the border, Reuters reported, citing Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee. However, even if such legislation passes Congress, Trump could veto it. Overriding a veto would require a two-thirds majority in both chambers, making a legislative rollback difficult. Democrats could more immediately challenge Trump's trade agenda through congressional oversight. With control of key committee leadership positions, they could hold hearings and investigate the administration's implementation of tariff policies. Areas of scrutiny could include tariff exemptions for individual companies, the impact of duties on small businesses, and the implementation of investment commitments made by Japan, South Korea and other trading partners. Although such probes would not directly change tariff rates, they could increase public scrutiny and pressure the administration to explain its decisions. Democrats could also use tariffs-related votes and proposals to reform trade laws to shape the debate ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Greta Peisch, a former general counsel at the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, told Reuters that even unsuccessful legislative efforts could help lay the groundwork for a broader Democratic trade policy. At stake is the balance of trade authority between Congress and the president. Although the Constitution gives Congress the power to regulate foreign commerce and impose duties, successive laws have delegated some of that authority to the executive branch. Democrats' efforts to reclaim or limit those powers would therefore face significant legal and political hurdles, including Trump's veto power. While the midterm results could give them greater leverage to scrutinize his tariff policies, they are unlikely to force an immediate reversal of his broader trade agenda. ON TRANSATLANTIC RELATIONS While the Democrats' sweeping victory has raised hopes among some European leaders for the future of transatlantic ties, many remain skeptical that the election results will do much to bridge the widening divisions between Europe and the United States over trade, security and other issues. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky expressed hope that the Democrats' victory would translate into greater support for Ukraine in its war with Russia. In an interview with German broadcaster ZDF on Wednesday, Zelensky thanked Republicans for their support but said Democrats had been particularly clear in their commitment to backing Ukraine and strengthening ties between the United States and Europe. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said he expects cooperation with the U.S. government and Congress to become broader and more extensive, expressing hope that the change of power in Congress will bring new momentum to support for Ukraine. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store called the election outcome "a powerful political signal about a change of course among American voters," noting that voices more closely aligned with Norway's positions were emerging in American policy circles, particularly on climate, the environment and development aid. Nevertheless, concerns persist that political polarization in the United States will deepen, making its foreign policy increasingly unpredictable and complicating relations with the Europeans. Brando Benifei, chair of the European Parliament's Delegation for Relations with the United States, warned that Trump could pursue an increasingly erratic foreign policy over the next two years. His decisions on Ukraine and the Middle East, Benifei said, would have significant implications for Europe. "It would be a mistake for Europeans to assume there will be warmer transatlantic relations," even if Democrats gained control of Congress, warned Wolfgang Ischinger, chairman of the Munich Security Conference. If constrained by Congress on domestic policy, Trump could shift more of his attention to foreign policy and trade, Ischinger argued, warning that Europe should brace for "not more harmonious transatlantic relations but more acrimony and even more Trump demands on Europe." The election results should not distract Europe from "the vital and urgent need" to guarantee its interests, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said, noting that Europe must become stronger, more prosperous and more democratic. Ian Kenny, executive director of the John Adams Institute in Amsterdam, said divisions could emerge within the U.S. decision-making process, with the House of Representatives potentially taking a more active role in oversight. Therefore, he said, Europe might have to contend with "two very different realities" in its dealings with the United States. Peter Filzmaier, a political scientist at the University of Graz in Austria, urged Europe not to become blindly optimistic too soon. He noted that Trump could exercise his power to veto legislation and budget bills passed by Congress over the next two years, potentially plunging the U.S. government into political deadlock or even paralysis. The White House's current foreign policy and its broader approach to transatlantic relations are unlikely to change significantly in the short term, he said. ■

item.title: Dunhuang's creative products draw international visitors at Silk Road expo
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05
LANZHOU, Nov. 5 (Xinhua) -- At the cultural and creative exhibition area of the 9th Silk Road (Dunhuang) International Cultural Expo, a series of products blending traditional charm with modern design drew visitors' attention. The expo, held from Monday to Wednesday in Dunhuang, northwest China's Gansu Province, brought together around 1,200 representatives from more than 50 countries and regions. It featured forums, cultural exhibitions and artistic performances to showcase Dunhuang's rich culture and promote dialogue on global cultural cooperation. Dillon Thomas Longey, a 20-year-old student from the University of Central Oklahoma in the United States, and his companions moved from booth to booth, admiring Dunhuang-themed products with keen interest. Some bought postcards printed with mural patterns, while others were drawn to plush camels. "This is so cool!" Longey said, describing the integration of history and culture into modern design as a fascinating way to communicate. "Sharing Dunhuang's culture and history through these products is really great!" Because of a tight schedule, Longey only had time to buy a few postcards, but he hoped to choose more cultural products to take back to the United States for family and friends. Briana Corazon Donovan, a 22-year-old American student from the same university, was equally impressed. "Buying a product means you can take culture home with you," she said. These cultural and creative products from northwest China are becoming a window through which foreign visitors can learn about Dunhuang and experience Chinese culture. Dunhuang was once a hub on the Silk Road in northwest China. For centuries, merchants and envoys from different regions passed through, helping create a rich cultural heritage that includes the Mogao Caves. Today, from classic mural figures such as flying apsaras and the nine-colored deer to a wealth of Silk Road elements, ancient Dunhuang culture is being woven into daily life through modern creative design. Sun Xuehu, deputy general manager of Dunhuang Cultural and Tourism Group Co., Ltd., said that in recent years Dunhuang has continued to explore new ways to transform and develop its cultural heritage. Cultural and creative products have expanded from traditional tourist souvenirs into areas such as household goods and artistic design, while cultural consumption options have become increasingly diverse. The Dunhuang Book Center has developed more than 5,000 cultural and creative products. Visitors can read Dunhuang cultural classics while enjoying coffee and browsing products, and can also try their hand at copying murals. At the Dunhuang Press, visitors can make seals and experience woodblock rubbing, gaining a feel for traditional craftsmanship. Data show that in the first half of 2026, Dunhuang received 67,000 overseas visits, up 45.6 percent year on year. As Dunhuang attracts more foreign tourists, its distinctive cultural and creative products are gaining more overseas fans. Shen Hongjie, who runs a woodcarving painting shop in Dunhuang, said his overseas customers often show different interests: some are drawn to desert scenery, others to flying apsara imagery, and still others to relief works. At the same time, more cultural consumption spaces with international elements are appearing in Dunhuang. In the city's Nancang historic and cultural district, a commercial building incorporates images of Silk Road merchants and travelers into its courtyard design. Some restaurants are combining Dunhuang specialty ingredients with Western-style dining, offering creative dishes. Zhang Qi, who is in charge of the project, said that given the growing number of foreign tourists coming to Dunhuang, the project has incorporated international elements into its design and services and employs English-speaking staff. The aim is to provide a more comfortable environment for visitors from different cultural backgrounds to communicate and spend time. From exhibition booths to street-side shops, from traditional art to modern life, Dunhuang culture is reaching visitors from around the world in increasingly diverse ways. Behind these novel products and experiences, what truly resonates is still the appeal of Dunhuang culture itself. Russian scholar Nadezhda Zamyatina, visiting Dunhuang for the first time, is working with a research team from Tianjin University in north China on an urban planning study focused on Dunhuang. During the trip, she bought cultural and creative products such as Dunhuang-themed scarves and teacups. In Zamyatina's view, Dunhuang is an important meeting point of different civilizations, with a rich and unique cultural heritage. She was pleasantly surprised that Dunhuang has not only preserved precious historical heritage but also integrated cultural elements into urban landscapes and daily life, allowing people to touch the city's history in their everyday lives. "Many cities display culture on walls. Dunhuang also uses floor tiles and cultural and creative products to tell its history, which is impressive," Zamyatina said. She found the approach inspiring and hoped other cities would learn from Dunhuang's experience, and that more creative Dunhuang products would appear in the future. For centuries, Dunhuang witnessed encounters and exchanges among different civilizations along the Silk Road. Today, cultural and creative products that foreign visitors pack into their bags will carry Dunhuang's cultural memory across mountains and seas to a wider world. ■

item.title: World Insights: Democrats' win reflects U.S. voter discontent, unlikely to reshape Trump's Mideast policy
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05
by Mahmoud Fouly CAIRO, Nov. 5 (Xinhua) -- The Democrats' sweeping victory in the U.S. midterm elections reflects widespread dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump's domestic and foreign policies, particularly their economic costs, but is unlikely to fundamentally reshape his Middle East policy, political experts said. In Tuesday's elections, Democrats secured victories in traditionally Republican states, including Texas, Kansas and South Carolina, and gained majorities in both the Senate and the House of Representatives, ending Republican control of Congress. The new Congress is scheduled to convene in January. DEEP DISSATISFACTION Maged Botros, a political science professor at Capital University in Egypt, described the outcome as a "punitive vote" against Trump, saying voters were responding to rising living costs as well as dissatisfaction with his handling of foreign affairs, including the war with Iran. "The biggest determinant is domestic economic conditions," Botros told Xinhua, adding that disputes with other countries and the costs of overseas military involvement had compounded voters' frustration. Saeed Okasha, a political expert and researcher at the Cairo-based Al-Ahram Center for Political and Strategic Studies, said the results were "no surprise," given mounting economic pressures at home and Trump's declining popularity before the elections. "What drives American voters is the prices of goods and services," Okasha said, adding that "anger over Trump's foreign policies translated into domestic discontent, consequently affecting the congressional election results." Public opinion surveys underscored the role of economic concerns and opposition to the Iran war. A Reuters/Ipsos poll of 1,765 U.S. adults, conducted from Oct. 29 to Nov. 2, found that 48 percent of registered voters cited the cost of living as the top issue influencing their vote, compared with 26 percent who cited the state of democracy and 13 percent immigration. An NBC News national exit poll conducted Tuesday found that 63 percent of voters believed the United States had made the wrong decision in taking military action against Iran. It remains uncertain, however, whether such discontent will translate into constraints on U.S. military decision-making. Okasha argued that voters' economic concerns did not necessarily mean they would oppose military action against Iran if it were deemed necessary. Botros, meanwhile, stressed what he described as Americans' longstanding aversion to costly military interventions abroad. LIMITED IMPACT ON MIDEAST POLICY Despite the Republican setback, Democratic control of Congress is not expected to automatically bring about a major shift in U.S. policy toward the Middle East. "The matter is not as simple as saying that winning the elections means controlling American decision-making," Okasha said. He pointed to competing interests, powerful lobbying groups and divisions within the Democratic Party, particularly over national security and foreign policy. Laurel Rapp, director of the U.S. and North America Programme at London-based think tank Chatham House, told CNBC on Wednesday that while Trump would face greater constraints in congressional oversight and investigations, he would retain considerable latitude in foreign policy. Okasha said the Democratic Party's progressive wing might favor a different approach to the Middle East, but more moderate members were not necessarily inclined to pursue conciliatory policies on national security. Some Democrats, he added, could still support a hard line toward Iran. He also said Trump himself appeared to favor economic pressure on Iran over further military action. Botros noted that although the U.S. constitutional system provides for checks and balances on presidential power, Trump retains substantial authority through executive orders and agreements, as well as his veto over legislation. Control of both chambers will allow Democrats to block legislation, scrutinize the administration and influence spending decisions and appointments. However, overriding a presidential veto requires a two-thirds majority in each chamber, a threshold Democrats are not expected to reach, according to the experts. A Brookings Institution analysis published in late October noted that even with a new majority, Democrats would be unlikely to secure the two-thirds support needed to override a presidential veto. Ahmed Youssef, a political science professor at Cairo University, said the shift in the balance of power in Congress would have an impact, but a sudden change in the policies of a major country was unlikely. "Major powers base their policies on objective considerations," Youssef said, adding that Trump's confrontational approach and willingness to use presidential powers could lead to repeated disputes with lawmakers. "I expect the final two years of Trump's term to be full of confrontation between the presidency and the legislature," Youssef told Xinhua. "Confrontation, but not fundamental change."■

item.title: Global media leaders call for closer dialogue, coordination amid security challenges
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05
BEIJING, Nov. 5 (Xinhua) -- Chinese and foreign media representatives attending the 7th World Media Summit in Beijing on Thursday called for stronger dialogue and cooperation to address global security challenges and promote common development. A forum on powering intelligent media was held on the sidelines of the summit, bringing together participants to discuss how media can leverage advanced technologies, build consensus and contribute to global security and shared development. Ren Weidong, deputy editor-in-chief of Xinhua News Agency, said in his address that media outlets should not be bystanders or onlookers in the face of global security challenges, but should strive to shoulder their responsibilities. Media should serve as guardians of factual reporting, adopters of advanced technologies, disseminators of diverse voices and promoters of exchanges and cooperation, helping pool collective wisdom to safeguard global security and promote sustainable development, Ren said. Abdul Hakim, president director of Indonesia's Antara News Agency, said opportunities created by advances in energy infrastructure and computing capacity should benefit developing countries, and digital transformation should enable more people outside major cities to gain access to credible information. People should embrace innovation while upholding principles, and news production should be accurate, fair and honest, he said. Participants of the forum also called for stronger cooperation in sharing technological achievements and building professional capabilities, promoting the development of artificial intelligence in a safer, fairer and more inclusive direction. The 7th World Media Summit, co-hosted by Xinhua News Agency and the People's Government of Beijing Municipality, is to be held from Nov. 5 to 9 in Beijing. Under the theme "Media in the Intelligent Age: From Consensus to Action", the summit brings together nearly 500 delegates from nearly 330 mainstream media outlets, think tanks, government departments and international organizations from 112 countries and regions around the world. The mechanism of the World Media Summit was initiated in 2009 and is an important global platform for high-end media exchange and cooperation. ■

item.title: News Analysis: Canton Fair, CIIE in China highlight shared global gains
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05
BEIJING, Nov. 5 (Xinhua) -- The ninth edition of the China International Import Expo (CIIE), China's flagship buying platform, opened in Shanghai on Thursday, one day after the 140th Canton Fair, the country's premier export showcase, concluded in Guangzhou. Held back-to-back, the two events offer a fresh lens to examine China's foreign trade. DUAL FAIRS REFLECT CHINA'S TRADE FOOTPRINT The numbers of overseas companies and industry heavyweights attending the 9th CIIE are set to reach record highs this year. More than 300 Fortune Global 500 companies and industry leaders are expected to participate, marking a record high, while over 2,000 companies will be exhibiting for the first time, according to organizers. This year's expo has attracted a record 4,142 overseas exhibitors from 148 countries and regions. In total, 162 countries, regions and international organizations are participating, said China's Ministry of Commerce. On the banks of the Pearl River in south China, a steady stream of orders at the Canton Fair served as evidence of the robust global demand fueling China's export performance. China's total goods imports and exports reached 39.94 trillion yuan (about 5.95 trillion U.S. dollars) in the first three quarters of 2026, with exports at 23.2 trillion yuan, up 16.4 percent year on year, and imports at 16.74 trillion yuan, a 22.3-percent year-on-year increase, according to the General Administration of Customs (GAC). THE STORY BEHIND TRADE FIGURES Trade is not simple arithmetic. Behind the surging trade figures lies a long, interwoven division of labor across global supply chains. A country that is more efficient in a given industry, with more complete supporting capacity and faster delivery, will naturally attract orders. Look beyond the figures, and the fuller picture comes into focus: the surplus is recorded in China, but the gains are shared beyond its borders. The distribution of gains becomes clearer when a product's value chain is laid out. Vehicles built at Tesla's Shanghai plant, many of them shipped directly to Europe and Asia-Pacific markets, are all counted as Chinese exports. This happens every day, as foreign firms operating in China produce for the world. In the first half of 2026, foreign-invested enterprises accounted for nearly 30 percent of China's exports to the European Union, close to 40 percent of exports to the Republic of Korea, and more than 30 percent to emerging markets such as Mexico and Vietnam, according to customs data. Foreign firms contributed 27 percent of China's total exports in 2025, meaning roughly three in every ten goods shipped from China came from a foreign-funded factory. A product labeled "Made in China" may be designed in Germany, use key components from Japan and the Republic of Korea, draw raw materials from Latin America, be assembled in China's Yangtze River Delta or Pearl River Delta, and end up sold in the Middle East, Europe or South America. The product leaves China and the surplus is booked in China's accounts, but the profits are shared along the entire chain. Reading only the surplus without asking how value is distributed yields a partial conclusion. Volkswagen offers a case in point. After more than four decades in China, the group is shifting its strategy from "In China, for China" to "In China, beyond China." "Over recent years, China has developed into a global automotive export hub. Volkswagen Group intends to participate more strongly in this development. We want to scale the capabilities we have built here beyond China," said Ralf Brandstätter, chairman and CEO of Volkswagen Group China. Cars built in China by Volkswagen are already exported to the Middle East and Central Asia, with ASEAN and South America set to follow. The picture looks similar when viewing the aggregate data. In the first three quarters of this year, foreign-invested enterprises recorded 11.69 trillion yuan in imports and exports, up 19 percent year on year and a record high for this period, according to GAC. Trade in intermediate goods rose 27.4 percent to 7.9 trillion yuan, while exports of high-tech products jumped 42.1 percent. More than 150 foreign firms each handled over 10 billion yuan in trade, 20 more than a year earlier, GAC data showed. NEW DEMAND CREATES EXPANDED MARKETS Nor is the market seen as a fixed pie to be divided. Global renewable energy capacity is projected to nearly triple by 2030, a gap that requires vast amounts of clean energy equipment to fill. In the first half of this year, exports by private firms of the "new trio," namely electric vehicles, lithium batteries and photovoltaic products, surged by 45.8 percent. Solar panels, lithium batteries and wind power equipment, meanwhile, are meeting new demand from the global green transition rather than competing for saturated markets. There are more direct examples. Sustained high temperatures have pushed up cooling demand, and Europe's air-conditioning market keeps expanding, with European buyers traveling to Guangzhou to purchase in bulk at the Canton Fair. As more countries accelerate prefabricated construction and tourism camp development, tight housing supply and fast deployment needs inquiries at prefabricated building materials and modular housing booths have also grown rapidly at this fair. A BROADER VIEW OF BALANCED TRADE The surplus also needs to be read alongside the broader balance of payments. China runs a large surplus in goods trade, but deficits in services trade and investment income. Its current account surplus is roughly 3.7 percent of GDP, within the range widely regarded as reasonable internationally. China stands as not only a major seller but also a major buyer. Its imports reached 18.5 trillion yuan in 2025, making it the world's second-largest import market for 17 consecutive years and a major export destination for nearly 80 countries and regions, official data showed. China, notably, does not deliberately pursue a trade surplus and has consistently worked toward more balanced trade. In the first half of 2026, the nation's imports exceeded 10 trillion yuan for the first time in this period. COMPARATIVE ADVANTAGE BEATS ZERO-SUM THINKING The point of economic and trade exchanges is not a zero-sum contest but the use of comparative advantages to deliver development gains to every participant in the chain. Dani Rodrik, a professor at Harvard University, argued in a commentary in August that when major economies are running at near full capacity, trade deficits should not be a cause for concern. Such deficits mean deficit nations consume more goods supplied by surplus economies, a transfer of purchasing power from surplus countries. "Under the current circumstances, then, China's widely criticized surpluses might as well be called enrich-thy-neighbor," he wrote. As the Canton Fair wound down, many buyers headed straight from Guangzhou to Shanghai. Their itineraries show not simply that China is opening up, but that both ends of the supply chain, and partners along it, have something to gain. ■

item.title: Report highlights China's growing role as global import market
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05
This photo taken on Nov. 5, 2026 shows a scene of the launch of the Export-to-China Capacity Development Report in east China's Shanghai. The Export-to-China Capacity Development Report, designed to help other countries boost exports to China, debuted at the ninth Hongqiao International Economic Forum, held as part of the just-opened ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE). (Xinhua/Wang Xiang) SHANGHAI, Nov. 5 (Xinhua) -- China is now both a global production hub and a key source of global demand, with a growing capacity to absorb goods from around the world, according to a report released on Thursday in Shanghai in east China. The Export-to-China Capacity Development Report, designed to help other countries boost exports to China, debuted at the ninth Hongqiao International Economic Forum, held as part of the just-opened ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE). As household incomes rise and consumption patterns shift toward higher-quality goods and services, China has considerable room to expand imports of premium products, advanced technologies and services, the report says. China's import mix has evolved from one overwhelmingly dominated by manufactured goods to a more diversified structure encompassing industrial products, energy and raw materials and agricultural commodities, it notes. The report says that China's expanding demand for both high-end manufactured goods and primary commodities offers an inclusive market for economies at different stages of development. The report was jointly compiled by the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences' Institute of World Economics and Politics and the Division on International Trade and Commodities of the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD). It additionally delves into the export performance of 10 of China's trading partners, including Colombia, Kenya, Spain, Thailand and Britain, assessing their potential in the Chinese market and offering recommendations on how to boost exports to China. The World Openness Report 2026 was also released at this forum, warning that global openness is under growing strain amid rising trade protectionism, spreading geopolitical conflicts and profound restructuring of global industrial chains. In 2025, the Global Openness Policy Index stood at 0.7448, down 1.09 percent year on year, while the Openness Performance Index fell 0.9 percent to 0.7458, reversing the recovery seen in both 2023 and 2024, according to the World Openness Report 2026. ■ This photo taken on Nov. 5, 2026 shows a scene of the launch of the Export-to-China Capacity Development Report in east China's Shanghai. item.title: (CIIE) Xinhua Headlines: Super buyer China opens door to shared prosperity at import expo
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-05
* The ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE), the world's largest import-themed expo, opened in Shanghai in east China on Thursday, just a day after the export-focused Canton Fair concluded in south China's Guangzhou, shifting the spotlight to China's increasingly prominent role as a global super buyer. * The CIIE's magnetic pull stems from China's growing role as a global super buyer, underpinned by its 1.4-billion population, its people's rising purchasing power and their growing appetite for a better quality of life. * Exhibitors at the CIIE, including those with a long-standing presence in the country, increasingly see China as more than just a consumer market. It is also a testing ground for innovation and a launchpad for products that aspire to reach consumers worldwide. SHANGHAI, Nov. 5 (Xinhua) -- Amid rising protectionism and waning faith in free trade, China is staging two major international trade expos back-to-back, signaling its steadfast commitment to continuous opening up. The ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE), the world's largest import-themed expo, opened in Shanghai in east China on Thursday, just a day after the export-focused Canton Fair concluded in south China's Guangzhou, shifting the spotlight to China's increasingly prominent role as a global super buyer. Running from Nov. 5 to 10, this year's CIIE has attracted 4,142 overseas exhibitors. With Canada and Sri Lanka as guest countries of honor, the ninth edition of the expo features more than 300 Fortune Global 500 companies and industry leaders. Across the bustling expo floor in Shanghai, sprawling over a total area of 440,000 square meters, exhibits range from cutting-edge technologies, such as a 6G terminal prototype and a high-precision turn-mill machine, to everyday consumer goods, including food, cosmetics and clothing, ready to test their potential in China's supersized market. MAGNETIC CIIE In 2018, as China's per capita GDP approached the 10,000-USD mark, the country launched the CIIE, a trade fair dedicated to imports, as a gateway for businesses to tap into the world's second-largest consumer market. Over the years, many innovative drugs exhibited at the CIIE have seen their market entry into China accelerated. Exotic food exhibits, meanwhile, have since enjoyed the media spotlight and found their way onto Chinese dining tables. According to Shanghai Customs, since the inaugural CIIE, more than 100 varieties of fruit from over 40 countries have gained access to the Chinese market. Once exotic fruits, from Malaysian durians to Peruvian blueberries, are now a common sight on Chinese supermarket shelves. For many exhibitors, the tangible benefits of past participation keep them coming back year after year. This year, nearly 200 businesses and institutions are returning for their ninth consecutive CIIE. One such "full-attendance" exhibitor, U.S. materials science giant Dow, values CIIE as a platform to "showcase its capabilities, understand market needs and expand value-chain partnerships," Puay Koon Chia, Dow Asia Pacific president, told Xinhua. Opportunities created by the platform have also reached many small businesses that have traditionally struggled to enter unfamiliar foreign markets. Ali Faiz, a carpet dealer from Afghanistan, first attended the CIIE in 2020 with just 20 or so carpets. Since then, orders from China have helped improve the livelihoods of more than 1,500 carpet-weaving families in his home country. To help exhibitors navigate market opportunities, this year's CIIE has built on existing initiatives, such as buyer-seller matchmaking events, the Hongqiao International Economic Forum, and a range of dialogues and cultural activities. It has also introduced new features, including a dedicated exhibition section for time-honored national brands from around the world. SUPER BUYER CHINA The CIIE's magnetic pull stems from China's growing role as a global super buyer, underpinned by its 1.4-billion population, its people's rising purchasing power and their growing appetite for a better quality of life. China has remained the world's second-largest import market for 17 consecutive years, with its total imports exceeding 90 trillion yuan (about 13.4 trillion U.S. dollars) during the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025). The pace is picking up. China's imports reached 16.7 trillion yuan in the first nine months of 2026, up 22.3 percent, the fastest growth since 2021. Beyond a supersized market, more sophisticated consumer demand in China is creating fresh opportunities for global businesses. From healthier diets and beauty products to outdoor sports and leisure experiences, China's growing middle-income population is embracing new lifestyles and driving demand for a wider range of goods and services. A newcomer to the CIIE, outdoor apparel brand Arc'teryx has gained momentum in China in recent years. John Yin, senior vice president-general manager of Arc'teryx Greater China, cited the country's thriving outdoor sports culture as among the underlying drives for the company's "longstanding commitment to China's market." A classic example of an emerging lifestyle in China reshaping global trade is the import of coffee beans. Long known for its tea-drinking traditions, China has emerged as one of the world's fastest-growing coffee markets. As coffee culture spreads from major cities to smaller towns, surging demand is driving imports of coffee beans from growing regions around the globe. For African coffee exporters, from Ethiopia to Mauritius, the CIIE offers a gateway to this swiftly expanding market. Adding to their optimism is China's zero-tariff treatment of imports from all 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic relations, which took effect on May 1. This year's CIIE features an upgraded Asia-Africa products zone designed to help African countries capitalize on the zero-tariff policy, while expanding free exhibition space for the least developed countries by 17 percent. Beyond the expo, China's commitment to opening its market wider is also reflected in its policy blueprint. Promoting balanced growth in imports and exports has been written into the outline of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030). Meanwhile, this year's government work report calls for boosting imports to promote balanced trade. This goal also aligns with a shift in domestic economic priorities that sees consumption taking on a greater role as a stabilizing anchor and key driver of growth. China this year laid out its first five-year plan dedicated to expanding consumption, setting a goal of raising total retail sales of consumer goods to around 60 trillion yuan by 2030. According to Sourabh Gupta, a senior fellow at the Institute for China-America Studies, the CIIE sends two important messages: China's commitment to a more balanced, higher-quality growth model driven primarily by domestic demand, and its willingness to become as impressive an importer as it is an exporter, thereby contributing to global economic rebalancing. "TEST GROUND AND A GYM" Exhibitors at the CIIE, including those with a long-standing presence in the country, increasingly see China as more than just a consumer market. It is also a testing ground for innovation and a launchpad for products that aspire to reach consumers worldwide. "China is both a test ground and a gym, a place where we test new ideas, challenge ourselves and continuously strengthen our innovation capabilities," Jay Wu, Michelin China vice president, director of government relations and strategy, told Xinhua. He noted that new trends and technologies in sectors ranging from electric vehicles to autonomous driving often emerge in China ahead of other markets. Unveiling a tire made with 75 percent renewable and recycled materials at the CIIE, the French tire manufacturer described its evolving approach to China as a shift from "In China, for China" to "With China, for the World." This shift reflects a broader trend among multinational companies. At a press conference in October, a Chinese National Bureau of Statistics official said more foreign firms are embracing "China Opportunity 2.0" by integrating more deeply into the country's industrial and innovation chains. The trend extends beyond industrial manufacturing to consumer goods, where increasingly sophisticated Chinese consumers are helping shape global innovation. Stéphane de La Faverie, president and CEO of the Estée Lauder Companies, noted in his videotaped message to the CIIE that as China continues to set the pace for beauty innovation, the country is not only an important market, but also "a source of talent, insight and inspiration." Maziar Mike Doustdar, president and CEO of Novo Nordisk, echoed his view. "China is becoming an increasingly important source of innovation. We are excited to bring China-originated innovation into our growing pipeline and explore its potential to benefit patients worldwide." For the Danish pharmaceutical giant, which has participated in every edition of the CIIE, China's rapidly evolving pharmaceutical innovation landscape and expanding healthcare market have reinforced its confidence in investing in the country. As Doustdar put it: "Investing in China is investing in the future." (Video reporters: Chen Jie, Sun Qing; Video editors: Hong Liang, Zhu Cong and Zheng Qingbin.) ■
